body_md:
Suppose that $a_f(r)^2=a_g(r)^2$ for all but finitely many primes $r$.
Then we must have $f=g$ by Proposition \ref{prop:separationthm}, a contradiction. The second assertion is from \eqref{eq:normalizedcoeff}.

label: eq:productbounds
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $u_i(r)\in[-2,2]$, write $u_i(r)=2\cos\theta_{i,r}$ with
$\theta_{i,r}\in\mathbb R$. Then
\begin{align*}
 1-u_i(r)e r^{-w}+e^2r^{-2w}
 =(1-e\exp(\mathrm{i}\theta_{i,r})r^{-w})
  (1-e\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta_{i,r})r^{-w}),
\end{align*}
where both factors are nonzero, since $|e r^{-w}|\leq r^{-\sigma}<1$.
The triangle inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 (1+r^{-\sigma})^{-2}\leq |V_{i,r}(e)|
 \leq(1-r^{-\sigma})^{-2}.
\end{align*}
Put $a_{i,r}(e)=V_{i,r}(e)-1$. Then
\begin{align*}
 |a_{i,r}(e)|
 \leq\frac{2r^{-\sigma}+r^{-2\sigma}}{(1-r^{-\sigma})^2}
 \leq C_\sigma r^{-\sigma},
 \qquad
 C_\sigma:=\frac{2+2^{-\sigma}}{(1-2^{-\sigma})^2},
\end{align*}
uniformly in $i$ and $e$.
Since $\sigma>1$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_r r^{-\sigma}\leq\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}n^{-\sigma}<\infty,
 \qquad
 \sum_r|a_{i,r}(e_r)|
 \leq C_\sigma\sum_r r^{-\sigma}=:A_\sigma<\infty.
\end{align*}
Thus, $Y_i(\boldsymbol{e})=\prod_r(1+a_{i,r}(e_r)) $ converges absolutely, independently of $\boldsymbol{e}$. The non-vanishing of $Y_i(\boldsymbol{e})$ is from the fact that
\begin{align}\label{eq:productbounds}
|Y_i(\boldsymbol{e})|&\geq \prod_r(1+r^{-\sigma})^{-2}>0.
                                                   
                                               
\end{align}


We now prove the uniform  estimate \eqref{eq:uniformtail}. Note that for any finite set $B$ of primes, we have
\begin{align*}\left|\prod_{r\in B} V_{i,r}(e_r)\right|&\leq\prod_{r\in B}|1+a_{i,r}(e_r)|\\&\leq\exp\left(\sum_{r\in B}|a_{i,r}(e_r)|\right)\\&\leq \exp(A_{\sigma}).\end{align*}
It follows that for $S>R$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \left|\prod_{r\leq S}V_{i,r}(e_r)
       -\prod_{r\leq R}V_{i,r}(e_r)\right|
 &\leq \exp(A_{\sigma})\sum_{R<r\leq S}|a_{i,r}(e_r)|\\
 &\leq \exp(A_{\sigma})\cdot C_\sigma\sum_{R<r\leq S}r^{-\sigma},
\end{align*}
where the final sum tends to zero
as $R\to\infty$, independently of $S$ and $\boldsymbol{e}$. Hence the
partial products $\prod_{r\leq R}V_{i,r}(e_r)$ form a uniformly Cauchy family. Letting $S\to\infty$
proves uniform convergence and \eqref{eq:uniformtail}.


Finally, give $\{-1,0,1\}^{\{\text{primes}\}}$ the product topology,
with each factor discrete. Then $\{-1,0,1\}^{\{\text{primes}\}}$ is compact by Tychonoff's Theorem. Each finite Euler product $\prod_{r\leq R}V_{i,r}(e_r)$ depends on only
finitely many coordinates and is therefore continuous. Uniform
convergence shows that $Y$ is continuous. Since the domain of $Y$ is compact, the image $K$ is compact. Finally, by \eqref{eq:productbounds},
$K\subseteq(\mathbb C^\times)^d$. This completes the proof.

label: lem:blockconditioning
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\Omega=\Omega_B\times\Omega_{B^c}$ and
$\mu=\mu_B\otimes\mu_{B^c}$, where
$\Omega_B=\{-1,1\}^B$ and $\mu_B(\{\eta\})=2^{-|B|}$.
The function
\begin{align*}
 g(\xi)=2^{-|B|}\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_B}\mathbf1_A(\eta,\xi)
\end{align*}
is measurable on $\Omega_{B^c}$.
Note that every $C\in\mathcal G_B$ has the form $\Omega_B\times D$ for a
measurable set $D\subseteq\Omega_{B^c}$, and
\begin{align*}
 \int_C g\,d\mu
 =2^{-|B|}\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_B}
   \int_D\mathbf1_A(\eta,\xi)\,d\mu_{B^c}(\xi)
 =\mu(A\cap C).
\end{align*}
Thus, $g$ has the defining property of $\mu(A\mid\mathcal G_B)$.

label: lem:tensors
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tensors}
For each pair $1\leq i<j\leq d$, choose a prime $r_{ij}$, with all
$\binom d2$ primes distinct, and put $B=\{r_{ij}:i<j\}$. For every
$r\in B$ and $1\leq i\leq d$, let
$v_{i,r}:\{-1,1\}\to\mathbb C$ be a nonzero function. Suppose that
$v_{i,r_{ij}}$ and $v_{j,r_{ij}}$ are not proportional for every $i<j$.
Then the following functions on the vectors
$\eta=(\eta_r)_{r\in B}\in\{-1,1\}^{B}$ are linearly independent:
\begin{align*}
 F_i(\eta)=\prod_{r\in B}v_{i,r}(\eta_r)
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq d).
\end{align*}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $d=1$, we have $B=\varnothing$ and hence $F_1\equiv1$,
so $\{F_1\}$ is linearly independent. Suppose $d\geq2$ and
$\sum_{k=1}^d a_kF_k=0$.
Fix $i$. We construct a linear functional $L_i$ such that 
$L_i(F_k)=0$ for $k\neq i$ and $L_i(F_i)\neq0$.

Write $r_{ji}=r_{ij}$. For $r=r_{ij}$ with $j\neq i$, define a
linear functional on the vector space of functions $h:\{-1,1\}\to\mathbb C$ by
\begin{align*}
 \ell_r(h)=v_{j,r}(-1)h(1)-v_{j,r}(1)h(-1).
\end{align*}
It follows that $\ell_r(v_{j,r})=0$, and
$
 \ell_r(v_{i,r})
 =v_{j,r}(-1)v_{i,r}(1)-v_{j,r}(1)v_{i,r}(-1)\neq0$
since $v_{i,r}$ and $v_{j,r}$ are not proportional. At every remaining coordinate $r\in B$, choose
$e_r\in\{-1,1\}$ with $v_{i,r}(e_r)\neq0$ and set
$\ell_r(h)=h(e_r)$. Such a sign exists since $v_{i,r}$ is a nonzero
function. Because the primes $r_{ij}$ are distinct, $\ell_r$ is well-defined.                                                          
For convenience, we write
$\ell_r(h)=b_r(1)h(1)+b_r(-1)h(-1)$. We define a linear functional
\begin{align*}
 L_i(H)=\sum_{\eta\in\{-1,1\}^{B}}
 \left(\prod_{r\in B}b_r(\eta_r)\right)H(\eta)
\end{align*}
for functions $H:\{-1,1\}^{B}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$. It follows that
\begin{align*}
 L_i(F_k)
 &=\sum_{\eta\in\{-1,1\}^{B}}
       \prod_{r\in B}\bigl(b_r(\eta_r)v_{k,r}(\eta_r)\bigr)\\
 &=\prod_{r\in B}\left(\sum_{e\in\{-1,1\}}b_r(e)v_{k,r}(e)\right)
  \\&=\prod_{r\in B}\ell_r(v_{k,r}),
\end{align*}
which is nonzero when $k=i$ and zero otherwise.  Applying $L_i$ to the relation $\sum_{k=1}^d a_kF_k=0$ gives
$a_iL_i(F_i)=0$, hence $a_i=0$. Repeating this for each $i$
proves the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $w=s-(k-1)/2$ and $u_i(r)=\lambda_{f_i}(r)$.
Then $\operatorname{Re}(w)>1$, $u_i(r)\in[-2,2]$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:separation} gives the condition \eqref{eq:abstractseparation}.
By \eqref{eq:standardproduct}, the products in
Proposition~\ref{prop:primeproducts} are $Y_i(p)=L(f_i,\chi_p,s)$.
For $h=\sum_{i=1}^d c_if_i$, the absolute convergence of $Y_i(p)$ gives
\begin{align*}
 L(h,\chi_p,s)=\sum_{i=1}^d c_iY_i(p).
\end{align*}
Since $h\neq0$ exactly when $\boldsymbol{c}\neq0$, we have 
$$\sup_{0\neq h\in S_k}
 \#\{p\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X):L(h,\chi_p,s)=0\}= \sup_{\boldsymbol{c}\neq0}
 \#\{p\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X):\boldsymbol{c}\cdot Y(p)=0\}.$$
Thus, the result follows from
\eqref{eq:abstractuniform}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $w=s-k+1$ and $u_i(r)=b_{f_i}(r)$.
Then again we have $\operatorname{Re}(w)>1$, $u_i(r)\in[-2,2]$ by
\eqref{eq:normalizedcoeff}, and Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}
gives \eqref{eq:abstractseparation}. For the corresponding
products $Y_i(p)$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:primeproducts},
\eqref{eq:reducedsym} gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i=1}^d c_iL(\operatorname{Sym}^2f_i,\chi_p,s)
 =L(w,\chi_p)\sum_{i=1}^d c_iY_i(p),
\end{align*}
where $L(w,\chi_p)\neq0$. Thus, $\sum_{i=1}^d c_iL(\operatorname{Sym}^2f_i,\chi_p,s)$ vanishes exactly
when $\sum_{i=1}^d c_iY_i(p)=0$. Taking the supremum over
$\boldsymbol{c}\neq0$ and applying \eqref{eq:abstractuniform} proves
\eqref{eq:symuniform}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $b\in\{1,3\}$, $m\in\{1,2\}$, and $s\in\mathbb C$ with
$\operatorname{Re}(s)>\sigma_m$. Put
\begin{align*} v(p)&=(L^{(m)}(f_1,\chi_p,s),\ldots,L^{(m)}(f_d,\chi_p,s))^T
,\\
 B_X&=\sup_{\boldsymbol{c}\neq0}
 \#\{p\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X):\boldsymbol{c}\cdot v(p)=0\},\\P&=P_b(X).\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq:standarduniform} and \eqref{eq:symuniform},
$B_X=o(P)$. 
Note that every proper subspace $W\subsetneq\mathbb C^d$ is contained in
$\{z:\boldsymbol{c}\cdot z=0\}$ for some $\boldsymbol{c}\neq0$. Hence
\[
 \#\{p\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X):v(p)\in W\}\le B_X
 \qquad(W\subsetneq\mathbb C^d).
\]
Since each coordinate of $v(p)$ is a nonzero Euler product,  the
case $d=1$ is immediate. Now we assume $d\ge2$. If the matrix with
columns $v(p_1),\ldots,v(p_d)$ is singular, then there is a smallest
 index $j\in\{2,\ldots,d\}$ such that 
$v(p_1),\ldots,v(p_{j-1})$ are linearly independent and 
 $v(p_j)\in
 W:=\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{v(p_1),\ldots,v(p_{j-1})\}.$
Fix this index $j$. There are at most $P^{j-1}$ ordered choices
of the preceding primes $p_1,\ldots,p_{j-1}$ whose corresponding columns  
$v(p_1),\ldots,v(p_{j-1})$ are linearly independent. For each such choice, $\dim W=j-1<d$, so at most
$B_X$ primes can be chosen for $p_j$. This bound is independent
of the preceding choices. The remaining primes
$p_{j+1},\ldots,p_d$ can be chosen in $P^{d-j}$ ways.
Therefore, the number of  tuples $(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ whose first dependence
occurs at $j$ is at most
$$
 P^{j-1}B_XP^{d-j}=B_XP^{d-1}.$$
Summing over the possible indices of $j$ gives
\[
 \#\{(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X)^d:
       \det(v(p_1),\ldots,v(p_d))=0\}
 \le (d-1)B_XP^{d-1}=o(P^d).
\]

Finally, let $T$ be a fixed finite collection of pairs $(m,s)$ with $m\in\{1,2\}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(s)>\sigma_m$. For each $(m,s)\in T$, let 
$$E_{m,s}(X)=\left\{(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X)^d:
 \det(L^{(m)}(f_i,\chi_{p_j},s))_{1\leq i,j\leq d}=0\right\}.$$
The preceding argument gives
$\#E_{m,s}(X)=o(P^d)$. Since $T$ is fixed and finite,
\[
 \#\bigcup_{(m,s)\in T}E_{m,s}(X)
 \le \sum_{(m,s)\in T}\#E_{m,s}(X)
 =o(P^d).
\]
Outside the above union, the determinants are nonzero for every
$(m,s)\in T$. Thus, the proof is complete.

label: def:relativedensity
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:relativedensity}
For $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathscr P_{4,b}$, put
$A(X)=\#(\mathcal A\cap[1,X])$. Its upper and lower relative densities are
\begin{align*}
 \overline\delta_b(\mathcal A)
 &=\limsup_{X\to\infty}\frac{A(X)}{P_b(X)},&
 \underline\delta_b(\mathcal A)
 &=\liminf_{X\to\infty}\frac{A(X)}{P_b(X)}.
\end{align*}
If these quantities agree, their common value is the relative density
of $\mathcal A$ in $\mathscr P_{4,b}$.

label: thm:kernelspanning
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that every proper complex subspace $W\subsetneq S_k$ is contained in
$h^\perp=\{g\in S_k:\langle h,g\rangle=0\}$ for some $h\neq0$.
By \eqref{eq:kernelpairing}, $K^{(m)}_{k,p,s}$ belongs to
$h^\perp$ exactly when $\mathcal L^{(m)}_{p,s}(h)=0$.
Since $h^\perp$ is itself a proper subspace, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 B_{m,s,b}(X)
 =\sup_{0\neq h\in S_k}
 \#\{p\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X):\mathcal L^{(m)}_{p,s}(h)=0\}.
\end{align*}
Thus, Theorem~\ref{thm:standard} gives \eqref{eq:kerneluniform} for $m=1$,
and Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetric} gives \eqref{eq:kerneluniform} for $m=2$.

For (i), fix $\delta>0$ and choose $X_0$ so that
$B_{m,s,b}(X)<\delta P_b(X)$ for every $X\geq X_0$.
For such an $X$, set
$W_X=\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{K^{(m)}_{k,p,s}:p\in\mathcal A_X\}$.
If $W_X\subsetneq S_k$, the definition of $B_{m,s,b}(X)$ gives the contradiction
\begin{align*}
 \delta P_b(X)\leq\#\mathcal A_X\leq B_{m,s,b}(X)<\delta P_b(X).
\end{align*}

For (ii), fix $Y>0$ and put $\mathcal A_{>Y}=\{p\in\mathcal A:p>Y\}$.
Removing finitely many primes gives
$\overline\delta_b(\mathcal A_{>Y})=\overline\delta_b(\mathcal A)>0$.
If $W_Y=\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{K^{(m)}_{k,p,s}:p\in\mathcal A_{>Y}\}\subsetneq S_k$, then
\begin{align*}
 \#(\mathcal A_{>Y}\cap[1,X])\leq B_{m,s,b}(X)=o(P_b(X)),
\end{align*}
which implies that $\overline\delta_b(\mathcal A_{>Y})=0$, 
leading to a contradiction.

For (iii), fix $\boldsymbol{p}=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)\in\mathscr P_{4,b}(X)^d$ and write
\begin{align*}
 M_{m,s}(\boldsymbol{p})
 &=(L^{(m)}(f_i,\chi_{p_j},s))_{1\leq i,j\leq d},&
 D&=\operatorname{diag}(N_1,\ldots,N_d).
\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq:kernelspectral}, the $j$th column of
$D^{-1}\overline{M_{m,s}(\boldsymbol{p})}$ consists of the coefficients of
$K^{(m)}_{k,p_j,s}$ in the basis $f_1,\ldots,f_d$.
Since every $N_i>0$, the kernels indexed by $\boldsymbol{p}$ form a basis
if and only if $\det M_{m,s}(\boldsymbol{p})\neq0$.
Corollary~\ref{cor:determinant} bounds the number of tuples with
$\det M_{m,s}(\boldsymbol{p})=0$ by $o(P_b(X)^d)$, proving (iii).

For a fixed nonempty finite collection $\mathscr T$ of pairs $(m,s)$ with $m\in\{1,2\}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(s)>\sigma_m$, put
\begin{align*}
 B_{\mathscr T}(X)
 =\max_{(m,s)\in\mathscr T}B_{m,s,b}(X)=o(P_b(X)).
\end{align*}
Using $B_{\mathscr T}(X)$ in the proofs of (i) and (ii) proves the
spanning conclusions for every $(m,s)\in\mathscr T$.
For (iii), Corollary~\ref{cor:determinant} bounds by $o(P_b(X)^d)$
the number of tuples for which $\det M_{m,s}(\boldsymbol{p})=0$ for at
least one $(m,s)\in\mathscr T$. This completes the proof.

label: eq:traceproducts
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $t_k(n)=\operatorname{Tr}(T_n\mid S_k)$ for the trace of the $n$th Hecke operator on $S_k$,  so $t_k(1)=d$, and set
$G_{k,m}=(\operatorname{Tr}(T_{a^m}T_{b^m}))_{1\leq a,b\leq d}$.
The Hecke relation gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:traceproducts}
 (G_{k,m})_{ab}
 =\sum_{\ell\mid\gcd(a^m,b^m)}
   \ell^{k-1}t_k((ab)^m/\ell^2).
\end{align}
Since $T_nf_i=a_{f_i}(n)f_i$, we have $G_{k,m}=V^TV$, where
$V=(a_{f_i}(j^m))_{1\leq i,j\leq d}$.
Since each integer $2\leq j\leq d$ is prime, the identity
$a_{f_i}(j^2)=a_{f_i}(j)^2-j^{k-1}$ gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:tracecoefficients}
 c_i(j)=
 \begin{cases}
 a_{f_i}(j)/j^{(k-1)/2},&m=1,\\
 a_{f_i}(j^2)/j^{k-1}-1,&m=2.
 \end{cases}
\end{align}
Thus, $(c_i(j))_{1\leq i,j\leq d}$ is obtained from $V$ by dividing
column $j$ by $j^{m(k-1)/2}$ for $2\leq j\leq d$ and, when
$m=2$, subtracting the first column from each of these columns.
Consequently,
\begin{align}\label{eq:tracecertificate}
 D_{k,m}^2=\frac{\det G_{k,m}}{(d!)^{m(k-1)}}.
\end{align}

The dimension formula of $S_k$ \cite[Theorem 3.5.2]{diamondshurman} gives the weights in the table below.
We evaluate the traces in \eqref{eq:traceproducts} by the
Eichler--Selberg trace formula
\cite[Theorem~2, p.~48]{Zagier1976}.
Besides $t_k(1)=d$, we need only the traces $t_k(n)$ with $n=2,4,16$
when $d=2$, and with
$n=2,3,4,6,9,16,36,81$  when $d=3$.
Substituting these exact trace values into
\eqref{eq:traceproducts} and \eqref{eq:tracecertificate} gives
the following values of $\lfloor16D_{k,m}^2\rfloor$:
\begin{align}\label{eq:coefficienttable}
 \begin{array}{c|rr@{\qquad}c|rr}
 \multicolumn{3}{c}{d=2}&\multicolumn{3}{c}{d=3}\\
 k&m=1&m=2&k&m=1&m=2\\ \hline
 24&158&22&36&1088&1\\
 28&101&51&40&748&267\\
 30&56&7&42&634&12\\
 32&78&58&44&635&316\\
 34&91&156&46&452&47\\
 38&68&18&50&542&3
 \end{array}
\end{align}
Since every entry is at least $1$, we have $D_{k,m}^2\geq1/16$ and
$|D_{k,m}|\geq1/4$.
